procedural_history.high_court_proceedings: The appellant applied to the Allahabad High Court under s. 561A of the Code of Criminal Procedure for the quashing of the proceedings pending against him before the Special Judge. The application was dismissed.

issue.issue_text: Whether a sanction under Section 6 of the Prevention of Corruption Act, 1947 is required for the prosecution of a person who committed an offence while being a public servant, but had ceased to be a public servant at the time the court takes cognizance of the offence.

facts: The appellant was a public servant at the time he allegedly committed an offence of criminal misconduct under the Prevention of Corruption Act, 1947.
Following a departmental inquiry, he was dismissed from service.
After his dismissal, the trial court took cognizance of the offence and prosecuted him.
No sanction under Section 6 of the Act was obtained or produced before the court.

The appellant argued that the court could not take cognizance of the case without a sanction, contending that his status at the time of the offence was the relevant factor, not his status at the time of cognizance.
law: Section 6(1) of the Prevention of Corruption Act, 1947, states that no court shall take cognizance of certain offences "alleged to have been committed by a public servant, except with the previous sanction" of a competent authority.
The court's primary principle of statutory interpretation is to first give effect to the natural and clear meaning of the words used in the statute.
Where a court has a general power to take cognizance of an offence, any legal provision that prohibits the exercise of that power must be strictly confined to its specific terms.
application: The Court analyzed the plain language of Section 6(1) and found its words to be "clear enough."

It determined that for the requirement of a sanction to apply, two conditions must be fulfilled: (1) the offence must have been committed by a public servant, and (2) the accused person must still be a public servant at the time the court takes cognizance of the offence.
The Court specifically examined clause (c) of Section 6(1), which refers to the sanction of "the authority competent to remove him from his office."

It reasoned that a person who has already ceased to be a public servant (due to dismissal, retirement, etc.) is not a person who is "removable from any office." Therefore, this clause, like the others in the section, can only apply to a person who is currently a public servant.
The Court concluded that the statute's language clearly links the need for a sanction to the accused's current status as a public servant who can be removed from office by a specific authority.

Since the appellant was no longer a public servant when the court took cognizance, one of the essential conditions for the application of Section 6 was not met. Consequently, the prohibition on taking cognizance without sanction did not apply.
reasoning.conclusion: The Supreme Court rejected the appellant's argument, holding that no sanction under Section 6 of the Act was necessary. The Court concluded that the requirement for a sanction applies only when the accused is still a public servant at the time the court takes cognizance of the offence. Since the appellant had already been dismissed from service, the protection afforded by Section 6 was not available to him.

arguments.issue_text: Whether a sanction under Section 6 of the Prevention of Corruption Act, 1947 is required for the prosecution of a person who committed an offence while being a public servant, but had ceased to be a public servant at the time the court takes cognizance of the offence.
appellant_arguments: The court should ascertain the intention of the legislature not just from the language of the statute, but also from the social conditions and the mischief it was intended to remedy.
Reliance was placed on decisions construing Section 197 of the Code of Criminal Procedure, which suggested that sanction was necessary even if the person had ceased to be a public servant.
It was argued that clause (c) of Section 6(1) applies to former public servants because, unlike clauses (a) and (b), it does not contain the words 'is employed'.
respondent_arguments: For Section 6 to apply, the person must not only have been a public servant when the offence was committed, but must still be a public servant removable from office at the time the court takes cognizance of the offence.

ratio_decidendi.ratio: For a sanction to be required before a court can take cognizance of an offense, the accused must be a public servant at the time the court is asked to take cognizance. The sanction requirement does not apply to a person who was a public servant at the time the offense was committed but has ceased to hold that office by the time of prosecution.
obiter: In construing a statute, a court must first give effect to the natural meaning of the words used if they are clear; only in the case of ambiguity is a court entitled to ascertain the legislature's intention by considering other matters.
Where a general power to take cognizance of an offense is vested in a court, any prohibition on the exercise of that power must be confined to the specific terms of that prohibition.

judicial_reasoning.core_finding: The conclusion is inevitable that at the time a Court is asked to take cognizance not only must the offence have been committed by a public servant but the person accused must still be a public servant removable from his office by a competent authority before the provisions of s. 6 can apply.
legal_tests_applied: In construing the provisions of a statute it is essential for a Court, in the first instance, to give effect to the natural meaning of the words used therein, if those words are clear enough. It is only in the case of any ambiguity that a Court is entitled to ascertain the intention of the legislature.
Where a general power to take cognizance of an offence is vested in a Court, any prohibition to the exercise of that power, by any provision of law, must be confined to the terms of the prohibition.
why_appellant_lost: The court rejected the argument to look beyond the statutory language to legislative intent, stating that the words in s. 6(1) are 'clear enough' and free from ambiguity, thus the court's duty is simply to give effect to the words used.

The court dismissed the reliance on cases interpreting Section 197 of the Code of Criminal Procedure, stating that Section 6 of the Act must be construed based on its own words, independent of any construction placed on a different statute.

The court rejected the appellant's interpretation of Section 6(1)(c). It held that the clause cannot apply to a former public servant because the crucial words 'of the authority competent to remove him from his office' presuppose that the person currently holds an office from which they can be removed. A person who has ceased to be a public servant is not removable from any office.

The court found that sub-section (2) of Section 6 does not support the appellant's view. It explained that this sub-section was added to resolve a different issue: which authority should grant sanction when a public servant is still employed but has changed jobs between the commission of the offence and the time of cognizance. It does not alter the primary requirement that the person must be a public servant when cognizance is taken.
why_respondent_won: The court accepted that the plain and natural meaning of the words in Section 6(1) must be given effect. The language clearly requires the person to be a public servant at the time of cognizance.

The court's interpretation centered on the phrase 'authority competent to remove him from his office' in clause (c). It reasoned that a person who has already ceased to be a public servant is not 'removable from any office,' making the provision inapplicable to them.

The court reasoned that Section 6 is a prohibition on the general power of a court to take cognizance, and such prohibitions must be strictly confined to their terms. The terms of Section 6, by their clear language, apply only to individuals who are public servants at the time cognizance is taken.
policy_considerations: The object of the sanction requirement is to protect public servants from frivolous or vexatious prosecutions so they can carry on their official duties efficiently. The competent authority is directly concerned and can refuse sanction if it is in the public interest to do so. This safeguard is for serving officials.
